title: ever struggled to complete a project?

posts.author: Vk9
posts.body:
So I've been working with RPG maker for already about 7 years, and with about 5 projects (which none of them were finished, although one of them is on current progress) and I've ALWAYS struggled with finishing the project, at the end, I change from working totally on that project, from giving up and not working on it.
I was wondering, is it just me? or is it a normal thing on giving up on it? since some of the main reasons why I do think this happens are because, one, it really takes quite a lot of time to make any project, and second, it's most likely to not end up worth it, because most likely people wont even play it.
I wanted to know what was your opinion on this, and if you have face this problem before

posts.author: TRIDIUM
posts.body:
Happens all the time, to pretty much everyone I've ever met.
Choosing a short, easy idea that you can get done and out the door is a great way to boost creativity. Sometimes I have to do that to get an idea out of my head that's distracting from my main project.
You can also descope your original idea down to something a bit more manageable.
As for being worth it, I wouldn't think about that too much. If all you want is for people to play and enjoy your game, than this is a great place to do that. Lots of people will give feedback and reviews (I do, although I'm a  bit swamped at the moment), so yeah, don't worry. You can also try advertising your game on reddit/twitter/etc.

posts.author: Eternidade_1
posts.body:
I was thinking about this the other day. I make a game so that I can play it first and foremost. I don't know if I can please other people with my game.
One thing that intrigues me is what do people do when they finish a project? Do they leave and never look at RPG Maker again?
The fact that they never finish a project leaves most makers trapped in the tool.
Do people really know the difference between developers and players? After all, the forum intended for developer support is not a forum for players. Which leads me to the question: why do complete projects appear out of nowhere, commercial or free, as advertising within the forums?
Excuse me for taking advantage of your post to include my questions.

posts.author: Arcaines
posts.body:
I mean, it depends on various things, what you making your project for, how well you planned it out and if you fully understand how much work is needed to make a game.
I was in the same boat, been messing around with rpg maker since XP era just before XV came out and yeah, made
so many
projects, just never finished them.
Looking back on it now, I understood why. It was either my project was Poorly designed, like I would make the games story as I went along so didn't have end in mind yet so poor planning on my end and probs as most people, did it for fun and it was, and as it is with most thing we do for fun. We get bored of them.
Now that I'm older I'm nearing the end of my first project, because this time, I didn't want to do it for fun. I wanted to make a career out of it and I feel I'm at a stage that I fully understand what it takes to make a successful game and I actually planned it out before hand so it had a end in sight. And the closer I got to that the more easier it felt to finish it rather then not knowing how many more dungeon I've got to do.
oh and the bigist thing was I made it manage and a lot smaller. Not thinking of making the next HUGE upcoming AAA RPG game.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
It's been taking longer than I'd like because of how much custom scripts I've had to write but on the plus side my programming skills have gotten way better.
If I never complete it I don't consider it a big deal as I've developed some useful skills. I've also had several people now asking for my code so maybe someone would buy the unfinished project for the codebase or to finish it themselves.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
I have a couple of points that might be reasons why that is:
Seeing your game as waste because "nobody will play it." Is a bad mindset to have imho. Make games because it's fun for you to make games. Nobody will play your game no matter what if you're not advertising anyway.
Maybe your projects are just too overscoped. Make small games. Set yourself a deadline. Cut all the bs. Make a game in 3 months max.
Stop giving up. Everyone has dry moments. Persistency is key. Work on your game even if you don't want to. Even if it's just for a little bit. Work on stuff that doesn't require much to do.

posts.author: BloodyKun
posts.body:
Well, I haven’t made anything much except one Mario fan game ages and ages ago, and a small jam project earlier this year, as far as game development goes.  I used to write a lot of fanfiction, but only ever completed maybe two or three.  My drawings are the only things I tend to get to a finished state consistently, and even then there are more longform ideas I take on such as a series of characters or comics, etc. that don’t cross the finish line.
I feel when it comes to creative endeavors, many people might seem competent and to just have endless amounts of finished pieces, but there’s a lot of stuff you likely don’t see any of at all for a myriad of reasons, whether it was not worth it to them to get further along or if they encountered a big problem or simply changed their mind about it.
Some think of their excess ideas as garbage to be filtered or recycled, and I think that’s valid enough, but I also like the notion that they are continuously refined, whether they are made into their own eventually or added to larger sculptures, without unnecessary bits.
What has actually helped me in the few times I’ve finished anything is not having the time to really mull over things and to just push through it.  Might lead to something more rough or raw at first, but I feel only then can you learn from your past experience and be truly rid of inhibitions and not be so afraid to test waters.

posts.author: Kizune
posts.body:
Always look ahead at the end goal. Ask yourself every time you launch RPGMaker, what do I want to achieve today and why am I doing this. What is it for and who is it for.
Is it to satisfy your creative energy? You make one scene or five maps or levels and bam, you've already achieved it. The brain will think, oh, it's done and that's okay if that's what you're looking for.
Is it for commercial purposes? Now you have to start thinking about target audiences, release strategies, social media, etc. Things to keep you busy and excited for your project.
Maybe it's a mix of both. In that case, you now have the creative freedom to make any story you want (with the limited knowledge you have now) and the end goal is to write, draw, research, and learn while balancing a feeling of responsibility to release your project to the potential players who may just be looking for the game you're trying to make.
Just know that at the end of the day, it's okay to stop if you no longer have the initial drive and it's a decision you've reflected on for a long time after considering the purpose of your project. What makes this accessible tool so great is that you can set your own limit and time to however you want depending on what the end goal is.
If you really like a project, you'll take breaks but you won't stop. When you finally find that one project you really love within you, not even the slog of automated programming can stop you. I suggest you keep doing what you're doing; and maybe take breaks to clear your mind. I go through the same process where I do a week without RPGmaker and them come back with a fresh outlook on what the next level would be. A refresher is always nice.

posts.author: Indinera
posts.body:
I don't particularly struggle. I have finished everything I wanted to finish. I do have a few unfinished projects but they never exceed ten minutes of gameplay, which is not a lot by my usual standards.
There is a dimension of struggle to finishing a game because typically, when you think you're close, you are probably not that close. You need to feel close about ten times to, well, really
be
close and in the position to finish the game. Mental resilience, persistence and passion for your work are the key elements in my opinion, what separates finished from unfinished.

posts.body: Well sometimes finishing touch is much longer than expected. When all jobs you feel comfortable to do are done, the rest require more effort but without them the project never feels complete.

posts.author: miragewolf
posts.body:
For me, I found often fixing a problem may lead to more problems. Wanting to keep a feature may require some other works currently not in use, which makes it scope creep.
Spoiler:
Old post by other user
https://forums.rpgmakerweb.com/inde...e-plugin-skills-are-bugged.69756/#post-662388
The thread is an example of such problems I had. To make it more difficult, I think the notification on official website is taken down but the feature is still there, so without a hint I had to turn off plugins in dozen to find the culprit since there was no lead what causes it.
There are also self doubts that are not actually related to personal projects/abilities, but game preference.  If games I enjoyed do not inspire similar games and are long dead, doesn't that mean no body would like it by default?
And trying to get better in art and writing by practicing feel like scope creep as well.

posts.author: teleshock_p

posts.author: LaCipolla
posts.body:
Two answers!
1. think if you never struggled to complete a project, you are not critical enough with your projects. If you want to make good art, you need to ask yourself: Is this good? Is this relevant? Should I put my short living years into
this
? (Ignore this answer if you do not have any such ambitions! ;D)
2. On the other hand, it is important to take a realistic stance with regard to your abilities, your life circumstances and your goals in this hobby, because all of these can become serious hurdles. And all of these are changing! E.g. daily life as an adult is different from what it is when your are seventeen, so it might be a good idea to adjust your process and the projects you tackle as you go along.
This ABSOLUTELY also means abandoning projects.
Also, my favourite tip always: Don't start out with huge projects. Finish small stuff first, and be it only so you can learn and KNOW that you can do this.

posts.author: inc0der
posts.body:
All the time. But a large part of the reason I've never released a full game in the last 10+ years or so of being a developer is that I just like making the building blocks more. Programming, art, music, I just happen to get dive deep into all fo the categories, especially programming.
With programming I can make random mechanics or small tools that help me with my day to day. Whenever I want to make a game, I end up just making mechanics, enjoying that and then moving onto something else.
I promise one day I will make a full game though, but for now I'm going to continue enjoying all the small steps on my way to the top.

posts.author: Hanakotoba
posts.body:
Heck I'm struggling to deal with mapping anxiety. It's my biggest bottleneck. I can't get how I want a map from my mind to look like in MZ.
I been thinking about hard capping myself to specific sizes for maps, and maybe they limit will make it easier.
I don't want a world map for my project so making interconnected fields can get rough when it comes to a lot like elevation not looking completely off.
I really wish RPG maker II mapping was still around. I feel my idea world is easier to envision in 3D.

posts.author: Quixote
posts.body: Very much so, I tend to start with stuff that really shouldn't be the focus at first. I was making one fangame that was just way too big with its mapping that I neglected every other aspect until I got tired of working on it. Something that has been helping me is the advice of "Make trash games when you first start.". Working on simple 5-15 minute games has genuinely been super helpful, and I can say I finally finished something for once!
